original_question: Which kinesin family gene that regulates the Hedgehog signaling pathway is mutated in the extremely rare autosomal recessive syndrome first described by Albert Schinzel in 1979?

final_qi.question: Which kinesin family gene that regulates the Hedgehog signaling pathway is mutated in the extremely rare autosomal recessive syndrome first described by Albert Schinzel in 1979?
final_qi.long_answer: Acrocallosal syndrome, an extremely rare autosomal-recessive disorder first delineated by Albert Schinzel in 1979, is caused by loss-of-function mutations in the kinesin family member 7 gene (KIF7). KIF7 encodes a ciliary kinesin that modulates Hedgehog signal transduction by controlling GLI transcription factor processing, so its disruption underlies the developmental abnormalities seen in the syndrome.

0.question: Which autosomal recessive syndrome was first described by Albert Schinzel in 1979?

final_answer.long_answer: The acrocallosal syndrome that Albert Schinzel first delineated in 1979 is an autosomal-recessive ciliopathy. Disease-causing, biallelic mutations were later found in the kinesin family gene KIF7. KIF7 encodes a ciliary kinesin that modulates the activity and trafficking of GLI transcription factors, thereby acting as a crucial regulator of the Hedgehog signaling pathway. Loss-of-function variants in KIF7 disrupt Hedgehog signalling and underlie the characteristic brain, craniofacial and limb anomalies seen in acrocallosal syndrome.
